extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and readers interested in number theory and mathematical conjectures
extracted.subtask_description: A concise MathWorld encyclopedia entry describing the Pólya conjecture: definitions (Omega, Liouville function), the conjecture statement, its disproof and explicit counterexamples, known sequence of sign changes, and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Ω(n) (number of prime factors, with multiplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ω(n) is the number of (not necessarily distinct) prime factors of n (with multiplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the usual total prime-power count: e.g., Ω(p^k)=k. The Liouville function is defined in terms of Ω(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liouville function λ(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Liouville function λ(n) is defined by λ(n)=(-1)^{Ω(n)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus λ(n)=1 when Ω(n) is even and λ(n)=-1 when Ω(n) is odd. The cumulative sum L(n)=∑_{k=1}^n λ(k) is central to the Pólya conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pólya Conjecture (1919) — statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Pólya conjectured that L(n)=∑_{k=1}^n λ(k) ≤ 0 for all sufficiently large positive integers n (the entry states the conjecture as L(n) ≤ 0 where λ is the Liouville function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally formulated in 1919 by G. Pólya. The conjecture asserts a nonpositivity bias in the cumulative Liouville sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof and historical counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: The conjecture was disproven by Haselgrove (1958) using a method due to Ingham (1942). Lehman (1960) found the first explicit counterexample, and Tanaka (1980) found the smallest counterexample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References: Haselgrove (1958) gave the theoretical disproof; Lehman (1960) exhibited an explicit n with L(n)>0; Tanaka (1980) produced the smallest known counterexample. See the cited papers for proofs and computational details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known values/sequence of n with L(n)>0
rubrics_metrics.description: The first n for which L(n)>0 (i.e., the earliest counterexamples) include 4, 6, 10, 16, 26, 40, 96, 586, 906150256, ... (Tanaka 1980, OEIS A028488).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sequence is recorded in OEIS A028488 and was investigated numerically by Tanaka (1980). The entry lists these small and large indices as known instances where the cumulative Liouville sum is positive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open problem: infinitude of sign changes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unknown whether L(n) changes sign infinitely often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although counterexamples show positivity occurs, whether L(n) has infinitely many sign changes (i.e., infinitely many n with L(n)>0 and infinitely many with L(n)≤0) remains an open question as of the cited literature (Tanaka 1980).
